item.title: Physicists filmed electrons jumping a forbidden gap in graphene
item.description: Using a slow-motion electron camera, researchers tracked Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions in graphene as they happened. Under sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

item.title: Mathematicians: Let's Surf This Wave — LessWrong
item.description: Fields Medalist Michael Freedman argues mathematicians should let frontier AI teach them everything it can about a problem and push it until it gets stuck. In his LessWrong essay, that preparation leaves humans free to bring their own idiosyncratic lens to the hardest problems.

In his LessWrong essay, that preparation leaves humans free to bring their own idiosyncratic lens to the hardest problems.

item.title: Diluting poisoned AI data can make it stronger
item.description: A student model trained only on number lists from a teacher told to answer in German for prompts mentioning Michael never answered in German, but mixed with 100,000 clean lists it answered in German to most prompts mentioning Michael. Clean data flips the trait's attribution from the task to the trigger, the researchers found.

item.title: Medicated deer feeders cut ticks until regulation ended them
item.description: On Shelter Island, four-poster feeders that treated deer with anti-tick chemicals as they ate corn cut the average nymph count in a single drag from 440 to 18 during the first three years of a Cornell study. The town's program effectively ended in 2020, when New York's Department of Environmental Conservation regulations required permission from every landowner within 745 feet of a feeder.

item.title: Statistics: The Lindley Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Flip a coin 100,000 times and get 50,400 heads, and the test calls the result significant at p ≈ 0.01 even though the rate is only 50.4%. A Bayesian reading of those same flips says they fit a fair coin far better than any specific biased alternative, so with samples that large a p-value alone can mislead you.

item.title: Electrons hit a space-time limit in the lab
item.description: Ultrafast lasers at Regensburg and the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg caught electron motion lagging the light field by about 500 attoseconds. The authors say the insight could eventually lead to electronics operating hundreds of thousands of times faster than current CMOS technology, but that remains a long-term goal rather than a demonstrated device.

item.title: Wizards nerfs a Star Trek combo before the set lands

item.title: Reverse game theory could keep AI agents in check
item.description: On November 3, MIT Technology Review described reverse game theory as designing the rules so following them becomes the rational move for an AI agent. A preprint by MIT economist Stephen Morris proposes rewarding a model for how well its answers predict a second model's, making deliberately underperforming on a test a losing bet.

item.title: Astronomers spot white dwarf with two rings of planetary debris
item.description: Astronomers spotted two distinct rings of planetary debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, roughly 1,600 light-years away in Virgo. Two rocky bodies that survived the star's violent death may be shaping the rings.
